patch.ref: html

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The snapshot's html element has lang="en", but all the page text is Portuguese (menus, titles, address, cookie notice). I checked the live server. It picks the lang attribute from the Accept-Language header: requests with en or en-US get <html lang="en"> with the same untranslated Portuguese content, while pt-BR gets lang="pt-BR". So a visitor whose browser asks for English, as Rampa's en-locale browser did, is served a page whose declared default language is wrong. Screen readers and other assistive tech would then read the Portuguese with English rules. The page's default human language is not correctly programmatically determinable for those users, so this fails 3.1.1. Visitors whose browser requests Portuguese do not see the problem.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Rampa's snapshot has <html lang="en"> and the page text is plainly Portuguese (menu, notices, footer address, link titles). I checked whether this was a collector artefact. With curl on 2026-10-24, the server (Orchard Core/Kestrel) sets lang from Accept-Language: it sends lang="pt-BR" for a pt-BR or empty header, but lang="en" for 'en' or 'en-US', and the content stays Portuguese. Rampa's English-locale browser therefore got what every English-locale visitor gets. That is a real version of the page whose programmatically determined default language (en) is not the language of its content (pt), so assistive technology would read Portuguese with English rules. The pt-BR version passes. The finding is a real 3.1.1 failure for the version served to English-preferring browsers.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The visible link text "English" in the language switcher is English, has no lang attribute and inherits pt-BR. Language links in their own language are the Understanding document's example for marking lang, so the visible text fails 3.1.2. Caveat: the Portuguese aria-label "Link traduzir para Inglês" is what screen readers announce, so the stated mispronunciation mostly does not happen. lang="en" should go on the visible text, not on the whole link with its Portuguese label. The visible-text versus name mismatch is a separate 2.5.3 issue.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: This is the "English" item in the language switcher, a javascript:void(0) link whose visible text is "English" with no lang attribute; nothing up to <html lang="pt-BR"> sets one. Understanding 3.1.2's example expects language names in a switcher to carry lang, which supports the finding. However, the link has aria-label="Link traduzir para Inglês", in Portuguese, so the name screen readers announce is in the page's language. The mispronunciation the finding describes does not happen, and adding lang="en" to the link, as it suggests, would make the Portuguese label be read with English rules. Only non-assistive-technology read-aloud tools would meet the unmarked visible word. A mismatch between the visible text and the name could also be a 2.5.3 (Label in Name) issue. Auditors would disagree on whether this fails 3.1.2.

auditor.rationale: The image is a lifestyle photo of assorted shop products (books, mug, toys, a 'Dig a Dinosaur Skeleton' box) in the 'Nature-inspired gifts for all ages' promo tile. It has alt="" inside an aria-hidden wrapper, and the live HTML is the same. The tile's heading, its paragraph ('Browse fashion, homeware and prints alongside puzzles and toys in our online shop...') and the 'Shop the collection' link already carry its message. The image only illustrates that text. The one kit is an incidental item in a mood shot, not information the tile is trying to convey. Treating the image as decorative is acceptable under the W3C decorative-image guidance and technique H67 (an image that only illustrates adjacent text), so this is not a 1.1.1 failure.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The img (alt="") sits in a div with aria-hidden="true" inside the shop promo tile. That tile's heading says "Nature-inspired gifts for all ages", its paragraph says "Browse fashion, homeware and prints alongside puzzles and toys in our online shop", and its link says "Shop the collection". The crop is a styled product photo: a mug, books, a dinosaur model, a dig kit, a puzzle cube and cards on a desk. It illustrates the range of gifts that the adjacent text already names. The one dig-kit box is incidental, not information the tile relies on. Hiding an illustrative image whose message the adjacent text already gives is an accepted way to pass 1.1.1 (H67, decorative or redundant image). The model treated a visible product detail as information that needed a text alternative.

message: The heading "Come curious, leave inspired" says nothing about the content under it.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: This h2 is the homepage hero banner's heading. The section under it lists the opening hours ('Open every day, 10:00–17:50') and 'Skip the queue with any ticket or membership', with links to 'Exhibitions and events' and 'Get free entry ticket'. 'Come curious, leave inspired' is a tagline, but it does state the section's purpose: an invitation to come and visit the museum, which is exactly what the visiting information and ticket links support. 2.4.6 asks that headings describe their topic or purpose, not that they be literal or exhaustive. A slogan heading that fits its content is not a failure, and the claim that it 'says nothing about the content under it' is too strict.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the visible hero banner's h2 (the other copies are hidden variants). Under it are "Open every day, 10:00–17:50", "Skip the queue with any ticket or membership" and two calls to action, "Exhibitions and events" and "Get free entry ticket". The heading is a tagline, but it is an invitation to come to the museum ("Come curious"), and the content is visiting information for doing that. So it describes the block's purpose, which 2.4.6 accepts as well as a topic. The finding asks the heading to name the content literally, which is stricter than the criterion. A tagline that matches the banner's purpose is not a 2.4.6 failure.
